blocks.content: Understanding exactly what determines a layer's cache key, not just that caching happens, is what lets you predict, and control, when a build will actually be fast.

Every instruction's cache key is derived from the instruction itself plus its relevant input. For most instructions that means the instruction text, for COPY and ADD it also includes the actual content being copied.

blocks.alt: Instruction text plus input together form the cache key

blocks.content: 2. COPY Is Keyed on File Content
blocks.text: 2. COPY Is Keyed on File Content

blocks.content: This is genuinely useful: Docker computes a checksum of the files a COPY instruction touches, so even if the instruction text is identical between builds, a change to the actual file content correctly invalidates that layer's cache.

blocks.alt: The actual file content, not just the command, determines the key

blocks.content: 3. RUN Is Keyed on Command Text Only
blocks.text: 3. RUN Is Keyed on Command Text Only

blocks.content: This is where a common gotcha lives: a RUN instruction's cache key is based purely on the command's literal text, Docker has no way to know that command depends on something (a remote file, an environment outside the Dockerfile) that changed. If the text is identical, the layer is reused, correctly or not.

blocks.alt: RUN cannot see changes to things it depends on indirectly

blocks.content: A RUN curl https://example.com/install.sh | bash instruction will happily reuse a stale cached layer forever, even after the remote script has genuinely changed, because from Docker's point of view the instruction text never changed at all. This is exactly the kind of case --no-cache or --build-arg CACHEBUST=$(date +%s) exists to work around.

blocks.alt: Identical text, stale layer, even if the remote source changed

blocks.content:
# A common workaround: force cache invalidation deliberately
ARG CACHEBUST=1
RUN curl -o install.sh https://example.com/install.sh && bash install.sh

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A layer's cache key comes from the instruction text, and for COPY/ADD, the actual content being copied as well.
RUN is keyed on text alone, which is why commands with hidden external dependencies (a remote URL, an outside script) can silently serve a stale cached layer.
